La petenera, melancólica y de origen incierto, se atribuye a una mujer de Paterna de la Ribera, «la perdición de los hombres», o a los sefardíes de los Balcanes; los gitanos la evitaron porque traía mala suerte. La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: Dick Clark's Vision for Rock History (1973)
facts.body: In 1973, entertainment mogul Dick Clark, at age 43, expressed a strong desire to create a movie that would document the 20-year history of rock music. This project, however, was never realized. "In 1973, Dick Clark, who was 43 at the time, said he really wanted to do a movie about the time, 20 year history of rock."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 47 - Dick Clark's Entertainment Empire

facts.title: "Bowie Quits" Concert (July 3, 1973)
facts.body: At the Hammersmith Odeon in London, Bowie staged a theatrical "retirement" for his Ziggy Stardust character, announcing that it was "the last show that we'll ever do." This event was captured by documentary filmmaker D.A. Pennebaker. Despite the dramatic announcement, Bowie did not actually quit, returning to the stage for a TV special less than two months later and continuing his recording and touring career. "Of all the shows on this tour, this particular show will remain with us the longest because not only is it the last show of the tour, but it's the last show that we'll ever do."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Legendary Gigs
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Killing Off Ziggy Stardust (1973)
facts.body: At the end of the 1973 Ziggy Stardust tour, Bowie announced to the audience that it would be "the last show that we'll ever do." While the public thought he was retiring, Bowie intended to retire the Ziggy persona to make way for a new one, Aladdin Sane. This willingness to "kill himself off" and constantly reinvent was admired by punks. "What he really meant though was that he was killing off Ziggy."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 1
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Prolific Output and Reinvention (1973-1975)
facts.body: Between 1973 and 1975, Bowie released an astonishing six albums in just three years and two months, including "Aladdin Sane," "Pin Ups," "Diamond Dogs," "David Live," and "Young Americans." Each record was different, making every release an event and keeping audiences guessing what Bowie would do next. "Album after album, single after single character after character two or after two or it was absolutely incredible."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 1
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Equipment Theft by Steve Jones (July 1973)
facts.body: During a multi-night stand at the Hammersmith Odeon in London in July 1973, David Bowie and The Spiders from Mars had microphones and amplifiers stolen by a young thief named Steve Jones, who later became the guitarist for the Sex Pistols. It is speculated that this stolen gear was used by the Sex Pistols in their early rehearsals and gigs in 1975, contributing to the punk rock era. "When Bowie and the spiders from Mars loaded into the Hammersmith Odien in London in July 1973 for a multi-night stand, a young thief named Steve Jones broke into the theatre and made off with a bunch of microphones and amplifiers."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Steve Jones' Theft of Bowie's Gear (July 3, 1973)
facts.body: Following Bowie's final Ziggy Stardust show at the Hammersmith Odeon in London on July 2, 1973, a young thief named Steve Jones (who would later form The Sex Pistols) broke into the venue. While a night watchman slept, Jones stole microphones, amps, and cymbals, some of which would be used to start his new band. "A young thief named Steve Jones somehow got inside and managed to help himself to whatever he could carry out, mostly some microphones and some amps along with a couple of symbols."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 1
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: 1973 Comeback
facts.body: 1950s rock and roll experienced a significant comeback in 1973, spurred by cultural phenomena like the movie "American Graffiti" and the TV show "Happy Days." This revival also saw contemporary artists like Elton John releasing songs in a similar vein, such as "Crocodile Rock." "In 1973, 50s rock and roll made a comeback. American graffiti, happy days, Elton John singing songs like Crocodile Rock, stuff like that."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 1: Punk
facts.name: Rock & Roll

facts.title: Formation and Marriage (1973-1977)
facts.body: Chris France and Tina Weymouth met in 1973 at the Rhode Island School of Design, where Chris was a member of a band called The Artistics. Tina joined The Artistics in 1975, and in 1977, they moved to New York and became part of the Talking Heads. They married in the same year they joined Talking Heads and have remained together ever since. "They met at the Rhode Island School of Design in 1973 when Chris was in a band called The Artistics. Tina joined the band in 1975 and in 1977, they moved to New York and became part of the talking heads. They married that same year and have been together ever since."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Couples in Music

facts.title: Elton John Gorilla Suit Incident – Richards, Atlanta, October 1973
facts.body: In October 1973, Iggy Pop and the Stooges were playing at Richards in Atlanta at the same time Elton John was touring America. Elton — engaged in a semi-friendly rivalry with David Bowie, who was a known Stooges supporter — decided to crash the show dressed in a full gorilla suit to surprise Iggy on stage. A photographer from Detroit music magazine *Creem* was tipped off. No one warned Iggy that this was planned, and no one warned Elton that Iggy was heavily intoxicated on speed that night. When Elton bounded onto the stage in the gorilla suit, Iggy genuinely believed it was a real gorilla, was terrified, and fled the stage. The incident was captured on film. After Elton removed the gorilla head and multiple people calmed Iggy down, the show resumed and the two performed several songs together — Iggy bare-chested, Elton still in the suit. "Iggy thought it was an actual gorilla. And this freak out is captured on film."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 100 Weirdest Things in Alt-Rock: Part 4
facts.name: Iggy Pop

facts.title: Elton John Gorilla Incident (1973)
facts.body: In October 1973, while the Stooges were on a punishing tour and Iggy was heavily incapacitated by Quaaludes, Elton John—dressed in a rented gorilla suit—surprised Iggy on stage at Richard's Club in Atlanta as part of a prank and a potential move to sign the band. Iggy, hallucinating, freaked out believing it was a real gorilla, and the band's guitarist James Williamson almost attacked Elton before his identity was revealed. "Elton John dressed in a gorilla suit, bounds on stage. Iggy, in his altered state and seeing triple, freaked out, thinking that this was a real gorilla."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Stupid History: The Music Version 1
facts.name: Iggy Pop

facts.title: Musical Influence (Post-1973)
facts.body: Iggy Pop was among the musicians whose work Poison Ivy and Lux Interior began to "consume" after being inspired by a New York Dolls concert in 1973. This reflected their growing passion for "anything that was sexy, wild, and played rock and roll." "Esto incluía músicos como al escúper, T-Rex, Ygpop, el acetado New York Dolls."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: Amor, Terror y Psychobilly: La Historia de The Cramps
facts.name: Iggy Pop

facts.body: RCA, John Denver's label, issued the compilation 'John Denver's Greatest Hits' in late 1973, for which he re-recorded several tracks. "his label, RCA, had issued a compilation. My beloved John Denver's greatest hits."

facts.title: Strategic Re-promotion of David Bowie's Catalog (1973-1974)
facts.body: As David Bowie broke on the album chart in 1972 with LPs like "Hunky Dory" and "Ziggy Stardust," RCA Records, his American label, strategically re-promoted his 1969 album (under the title "Space Oddity") and re-issued singles like "Space Oddity" and "Changes" in the early 1970s, crucial actions that solidified Bowie's career in America. "RCA Records, Bowie's American label, decided to re-promote his 1969 album, under the title Space Audity, with new post-Ziggy Stardust imagery and even a new video of Bowie miming the song in glam makeup."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Second-Chance Hits Edition Part 2
facts.name: RCA Records

facts.body: Can's 1973 album "Future Days" is credited with anticipating the post-rock genre of the 90s, highlighting the band's visionary approach to musical structure, atmosphere, and departure from traditional rock song forms. "y que se adelantó al por rock de los 90."

facts.title: Bum-Biting Incident – Buffalo Concert, March 24, 1973
facts.body: While performing a concert in Buffalo, New York, on March 24, 1973, a fan jumped out of the audience mid-set, screamed "leather," and bit Lou Reed on the buttocks. Security grabbed the fan and ejected him from the venue. Lou was forced to continue performing the rest of the show with a noticeably tender rear end. The incident reflected the kind of extreme, unpredictable audience behavior Reed attracted in New York underground circles. "Lou had to play the rest of the show with a rather tender button."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 100 Weirdest Things in Alt-Rock: Part 3
facts.name: Lou Reed

facts.title: Marrying a Woman Amidst Gay Presumptions (1973)
facts.body: Even though Lou Reed married a woman in 1973, many people continued to presume that his gayness was "the real thing." This perception was particularly fueled by the success of his hit song "Walk on the Wild Side," which openly featured real-life gay and transgender characters. "Even though he married a woman in 1973, many people presumed that his gainus was the real thing."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock
facts.name: Lou Reed

facts.title: Gorilla Suit Stage Crash (1973)
facts.body: In October 1973, Elton John, intending to prank David Bowie and potentially sign The Stooges, donned a rented gorilla suit and bounded onto the stage during a Stooges performance at Richard's Club in Atlanta. facts.title: KISS Formed January 30, 1973 at Popcorn Club, Queens NY – Real Names Abandoned; Makeup Ditched 1983, Restored 1996
facts.body: KISS evolved out of a glittery band called Wicked Lester. Stanley Eisen and Hame Whits (later Paul Stanley and Gene Simmons) recruited drummer George Criscuola (Peter Criss, who had been in a band called Lips) and guitarist Paul Frehley (Ace Frehley — renamed because there was already a Paul). Their first show was January 30, 1973 at a club in Queens, New York called Popcorn. Building on glam and glitter of the early 1970s, KISS adopted wild costumes and elaborate makeup, keeping their real appearances a closely guarded secret for a decade. After blowing up in 1975, they ditched the makeup on September 18, 1983 for an MTV appearance revealing their faces for the first time. The reunion of the original lineup in 1996 restored the old makeup designs. Paul Stanley and Gene Simmons retired in December 2023. "When they played their first show on January 30, 1973 at a club in Queens, New York called Popcorn, the legend began."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Pioneering Performances at CBGB (1973)
facts.body: In December 1973, band members Richard Hell, Richard Lloyd, and Tom Verlaine approached Hilly Crystal, owner of a bar named CBGBOMFUG, and secured a Sunday night slot for their band, Television, to perform for an admission fee of $1. After a challenging beginning, their performances at CBGB, combined with the earlier collapse of the Mercer Art Center, helped establish the club as the epicenter for New York's burgeoning punk rock scene. "Marina Half Weeks later, television played their first ever rock night at CBGB. And admission was $1."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: The Wall of Sound (1973)
facts.body: The "Wall of Sound" was an innovative and massive concert sound system unveiled by The Grateful Dead in 1973. It weighed 75 tons, stood three stories tall, was 100 feet wide, and required four semis and 21 people for transport. The system contained hundreds of speakers, specifically 568 JBLs and approximately 50 Electro Voice tweeters, powered by mostly Macintosh tube amps pumping out around 26,000 watts. Vocals went through one set of speakers while instrumentation went through others, arranged in "line arrays" for even sound dispersion. "The wall contained hundreds of speakers, 568 JBLs, and about 50 electro voice tweeters, to be specific, along with amplifiers, mostly Macintosh tube amps, pumping out something around 26,000 watts, which was absolutely insane for its day."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Concert Sound
facts.name: The Grateful Dead

facts.title: Cream Magazine Review (1973)
facts.body: A 1973 review in Detroit's Cream Magazine criticized Roxy Music's debut album, describing its artifice as potentially "unhealthy as the sheen on a piece of rotten meat" and noting Side Two's excessive reliance on Brian Eno's synthesizer, which "leans a little too heavily on the synthesizer... without the saving grace of drums and bass line." Despite the harsh critique, this divisiveness made them appealing to a niche audience. "From the drag queen on the corner, to the fop finery in the centerfold, to the polished deformity of the music on the record, this celebrates the kind of artifice that could come to seem as unhealthy as the sheen on a piece of rotten meat."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock
facts.name: Roxy Music

facts.title: Early Live Performance Critique (1973)
facts.body: Music critic Tony Palmer, reviewing a Roxy Music live show in the spring of 1973 after the release of two albums, called their albums "overproduced." However, he described the live performance as "demonic sinister apocalyptic, monstrous, dazzling flashy. What opera might have been in the 1970s had it not lost its nerve." Palmer's review also included a warning against the band resorting to gimmicks or selling out. "The group was, and I quote, demonic sinister apocalyptic, monstrous, dazzling flashy."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s
facts.name: Roxy Music

facts.body: This album recently marked its 43rd anniversary, an event tied to one of its three official releases. Its initial launch was considered a disaster, leading to multiple official release dates, driven by intense anticipation. The record company prematurely released the album before it was fully completed or out of post-production. The most significant official presentation, also commemorating its 43rd anniversary, took place at the London Planetarium, a venue chosen for its thematic alignment with the album's cover and overall concept. Despite the official presentation, the band, upset that the album was unfinished, boycotted the event. Specialized press attending the launch found only life-sized cardboard cutouts of the band members with the album playing, as the band refused to be present for its own release under these circumstances. Upon release, the album quickly reached number one on the charts but only held that position for a single week. Remarkably, it then spent approximately 15 years, or about 800 consecutive weeks, on the Billboard 200 list of best-selling albums in the United States, an extraordinary feat that, while not a record, came very close. It is recognized as one of the best conceptual albums in music history and a defining work in Pink Floyd's career. While the music itself is highly important, the band's primary focus during its creation was on the concept, not just the musical composition. The album integrates compositions, melodies, and even complete songs that pre-existed Pink Floyd's official albums, having been previously used in concerts but not recorded. The band aimed for a solid conceptual album with a very closed narrative, leading them to adopt a clearer and more direct lyrical language and to discard any material that didn't perfectly align with the album's themes. This represented an intensification of an evolutionary process within Pink Floyd, marking it as possibly their first truly great conceptual album and setting a new direction for the band's musical development. The complex development of its conceptual thread, rather than just the music, began almost a year prior; in February 1972, the band previewed a significant portion of the album's melodies and songs in London to specialized press and critics, who were amazed by what they heard but had to wait a full year for the album's release. The album's central concept is "the hardest aspects of the human condition." Two significant thematic influences were the mental deterioration of Syd Barrett, Pink Floyd's original leader, whose delicate emotional health and eventual retreat into reclusion due to severe mental problems (brought on by the band's success and record label pressures) deeply impacted the band's early career and ongoing exploration of madness and psychological evolution. Another important influence was philosophy, which the band began to seriously integrate as a mental thread and theme within their songs, expanding on their existing mystical and philosophical leanings. The album delves into themes such as madness (beyond Syd Barrett's specific case), hatred, greed, fear, consumerism, aggression, depression, and the fear of death, exploring these difficult aspects of human evolution throughout life. The album is divided into two parts, Side A and Side B. Side A approaches the harshness of the human condition from a personal and interior perspective: the first song addresses human madness or the loss of mental control; the second discusses regaining mental control and taking charge of one's life after losing direction; the third speaks of the refuge and reflection found once control is re-established; the fourth explores refuge and solitude after recovery and reflection; and the final song is an allegory of death at the end of life, once control has been regained. Side B examines the same themes but from a social viewpoint, focusing on how society and groups affect the individual. It touches upon greed, racial prejudice, consumerism, and the unhappiness induced by a society devoted to work and suffering. Side B analyzes this societal situation, offering a final conclusion, and again uses allegories, particularly mental illness, as a source of inspiration, but this time focusing on how a hostile environment can drive people to madness. Side B culminates in what the band called "catharsis," leading to a vision of liberation, a more humble understanding of the world, and a collective and cooperative perspective that champions unity for the common good over the societal competition that ultimately leads to madness and unhappiness. The album is musically incredible, considered one of the best in history, but its true significance lies in its profound conceptual nature, offering deep thoughts and a critical vision of society in the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s, marking a new, revolutionary way of working for Pink Floyd. "el Darkseller de Moon fue el último álbum que acabaron grabando Pink Floyd con capito de récord, se aparte de la isa que borrón pinta su relación."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.body: This iconic album featured early synthesizer experimentation, particularly on the instrumental track "On the Run." The band was intrigued by the new sonic possibilities offered by synthesizers, using a primitive model without a keyboard, the EMS VCS III. "If you go back to Dark Side of the Moon and the Instrumental Track on the Run, we hear primitive synthesizer, one without a keyboard called an EMS VCS III."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Post-Beatles Collaboration with McCartney (1973)
facts.body: George Martin, who built and ran Air Studios in London, agreed to produce the recording sessions for Paul McCartney's "Live and Let Die" theme. This marked a significant reunion, as it was the first time Martin had worked with a Beatle since the conclusion of the "Abbey Road" sessions in 1969. Martin later compelled the Bond producers to use McCartney's version as the title sequence. "Martin agreed to produce the sessions marking this as the first time since the end of the Abbey Road sessions that he got to work with a beetle."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Bond...James Bond...Music
facts.name: George Martin

facts.title: Producer's Ultimatum for "Live and Let Die" (1973)
facts.body: George Martin delivered an ultimatum to the Bond film producers regarding Paul McCartney's "Live and Let Die" theme. He informed them that if they wanted the "very good theme song," they would have to use Paul's version for the title sequence, otherwise they would need to find someone else for their movie. Faced with time constraints, the producers, either Harry Saltzman or Albert Broccoli, conceded. "When it was done George Martin went to the producers and said look we've got a very good theme song for you but the only way you're going to get it is if you use Paul's version as the title sequence."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Bond...James Bond...Music
facts.name: George Martin

facts.title: Death and Desert Cremation (September 19, 1973)
facts.body: Graham Parsons, former member of The Byrds, died of an overdose at age 26 on September 19, 1973, in room 8 at the Joshua Tree Inn in California. His body was then spirited away by his road manager from LAX to be cremated in the desert in a private ritual. A pile of stones known as Cap Rock is believed to be where the cremation took place. "This is where Graham Parsons, ex of the birds, died of an overdose at age 26 on September 19th, 1973."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Infamous Hotels and Hotel Rooms

facts.title: Retirement and Death (1950s-1973)
facts.body: Memphis Mini's health declined in the 1950s, forcing her to retire from music. A series of strokes eventually destroyed her ability to play the guitar, and she passed away in a nursing home in 1973. "For the decades, she would record many more songs, but declining health in the 1950s forced her to retire."

facts.title: Advertising Commercial for Old Home Bread (1973)
facts.body: Bill Freese, using the persona C. W. McCall, created a TV commercial for Old Home Bread. It featured McCall as a truck driver and a waitress named Mavis at the Old Home and Fillarepp Cafe. The commercial won a Clio, the highest award for an advertisement, and was noted for Mavis's seductive portrayal, which would likely not be made today. "That commercial won a Clio, the highest possible award for an advertising commercial or advertisement, and would never be made today as Mavis pretty much seduces C. W and kept him, quote, warm as toast while the blizzard raged outside."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 31 - The Spirit of '76 - Pop Music on America's Bicentennial
facts.name: C.W. McCall

facts.title: Fictional Artist Creation (1973)
facts.body: C. W. McCall was not a real artist but a fictional recording persona invented by an ad campaign for Old Home Bread in 1973. Bill Freeze was the creative director who conceived and voiced the trucker character, with Chip Davis providing the music, making him a unique commercial-to-music success story. "an artist who wasn't even real. The number one hit that resulted from this artist wasn't an ad in itself, but without advertising, the whole thing never would have happened in the first place."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: I’d Like to Teach the World to Buy Edition Part 1

"an artist who wasn't even real. The number one hit that resulted from this artist wasn't an ad in itself, but without advertising, the whole thing never would have happened in the first place."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: I’d Like to Teach the World to Buy Edition Part 1
facts.name: C.W. McCall

facts.title: Formation and Style (1973)
facts.body: Formed in 1973 in Rockford, Illinois, Cheap Trick were initially known for big hooks, similar to The Razberries, but their sound, largely due to guitarist Rick Nielsen, was more muscular, louder, and slightly more aggressive. They began by playing in various small venues like pubs and bowling alleys. "Cheap trick was formed in 1973 in Rockford, Illinois, a place just west of Chicago."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Power Pop

facts.title: Departure from The Wailers (1973)
facts.body: Peter Tosh left The Wailers in 1973, citing unhappiness with Chris Blackwell's refusal to support his solo work and a perception that Bob Marley, being lighter-skinned, received preferential attention within the band and from the label. "Tosh left the wailers in 1973. He was unhappy that Chris Blackwell would not let him put out a solo album and there were rumblings about the attention going to Marley."

facts.title: View on Country Music Diversity (1973)
facts.body: In 1973, Charlie Pride articulated a broad perspective on country music, arguing it is "many things" and the "basic music of America," encompassing elements of jazz, blues, and other categories. He believed that various genres were starting to "gel" into "one ball of wax." "Country music is just about time for it to stop being used as a whipping boy. It's good music. It's the basic music of America."

facts.body: Described as a "breath of fresh air" after the sonic intensity of "Tago Mago," this album moved away from darker sounds to explore a more atmospheric and cosmic aesthetic. It metaphorically takes the listener on a zero-gravity journey over the sea, drifting yet generating a constant sense of momentum, with Holger Czukay's magnetic tapes projecting luminous synthesizer notes. Considered the band's most balanced album, where no member overshadowed another, Damo Suzuki's contributions were less prominent and more discreet. This work profoundly influenced Brian Eno's ambient output and, indirectly, David Bowie's Berlin phase, serving as an excellent and luminous turning point for the band that anticipated the post-rock genre of the 90s. "Una obra excelente que aporta un giro hacia la luz a la banda y que se adelantó al por rock de los 90."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: CAN ｜ La Banda que (posiblemente) Inspiró a tu banda preferida
facts.name: Future Days

"MCA records, Newton John's American label decided to try something new. They would promote her next single to country radio stations first."

facts.title: First Album as Genuine Rock Star
facts.body: Released on April 13th, 1973, this was Bowie's first album as a "genuine rock star" and further developed the Ziggy persona into a "higher realm." The title itself, when separated as "A Lad Insane," hinted at Bowie's mental state and was influenced by his half-brother Terry's struggles with mental illness. "The next album, also called Aladdin Sane, was Bowie's first as a genuine rock star."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 1
facts.name: Aladdin Sane

facts.body: Bowie's mid-1970s character was named "Aladdin Sane," a title that reflected his mental state during that period, punning on "A lad insane." "No wonder Bowie's mid-70s characters was named Aladdin Sane."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt Rocks Craziest People
facts.name: Aladdin Sane

facts.body: One of Bowie's peak glam era LPs that topped the British album chart but did not hit number one in America. It was one of his last UK number one LPs until "Scary Monsters." "And though he hadn't had a UK number one LP, since the era of Aladdin, Sain, and Diamond Dogs, even Bowie's quirkier LPs from the Berlin period, consistently made the UK top five."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: Aladdin Sane

facts.body: Released in 1973, this album further twisted Bowie's alien persona and made his look even more iconic, notably with its album cover featuring a bear-chested, flame-haired David with lightning bolt face makeup and a teardrop. Although its lead single "The Jean Genie" wasn't a big US pop hit, the potency of Bowie's persona ensured the album sold well, leaping into the top 20 and hitting number 17 by June 1973. "And they were joined by a new album that put a twist on Bowie's alien persona and made his look even more iconic, Aladdin's scene."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 1
facts.name: Aladdin Sane

facts.body: Mike Oldfield's "Tubular Bells" was the first signing and release for Virgin Records, proving to be a huge hit. Its commercial success provided Virgin with the necessary funds to finance its expansion. "So Branson and his partners did, and their first signing was 2-biter bells by Mike Oldfield. That became a huge hit which allowed Virgin to finance an expansion."

facts.body: The title track from this 1974 album was so extensive it had to be split across both sides of the vinyl record. Part one ran for 25 minutes and 36 seconds on side one, while part two took up 23 minutes and 20 seconds on side two, making it technically not a single, unbroken piece of music. "Its title track was so long that it had to be divided into two. Part one ran 25 minutes and 36 seconds on side one. Well, part two took up 23 minutes and 20 seconds on side two."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: This album, released in 1973, revolutionized the music industry. Its immense success was pivotal for the foundation and growth of Virgin Records, contributing significantly to Richard Branson's fortune as it was the breakthrough hit for his nascent record label, which had started in the early 1970s. "todos lo conocemos porque en 1973 sacaba el grandísimo tubular bells con el que revolucionaba la industria de la música."

facts.title: Third Solo Album
facts.body: This album was released just a few months after the "Transformer" tour concluded and was initially met with widespread critical condemnation, marking a "great fall" for Lou Reed. It was a highly complex conceptual album, narrating the harrowing story of a drug-addicted couple living through their miseries in New York City, blending song and narrative. The swift composition period (less than a year after "Transformer," including an 8-month tour) likely contributed to its initial failure, as it was the first time Lou Reed had to create 100% new material without relying on Velvet Underground leftovers. "Realmente Berling era un disco muy complejo porque era una especie de algún conceptual que venía como anarrar una historia, venía a contarnos la historia de una pareja de droga dictos que vivían toda su vida o un poco todas sus penurias por la ciudad de Nueva York."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Tras los pasos de Lou Reed
facts.name: Berlin

facts.title: Critical Re-evaluation
facts.body: Lou Reed lacked strong instrumental knowledge for such a complex album and refused external help from other musicians or professional producers, which could have compensated for his deficiencies. While the album was "totally destroyed by critics" upon release, it has since been re-evaluated, with modern reviews from publications like Rolling Stone and Pitchfork being significantly more positive than their original scathing assessments. The album has gained "much context" and "charisma" within music culture over time. "Al final el disco acababa totalmente destrozado por la crítica."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Tras los pasos de Lou Reed
facts.name: Berlin

facts.title: Storytelling Style
facts.body: The album exemplifies Lou Reed's unique method of storytelling in his songs, where each track functions like a "small novel" or a "small, self-contained, everyday story" presented with novelistic depth. "Berlin" specifically defines his lyrical approach, concentrating a concise, novel-like narrative into a three-minute song. "Y es que al final yo creo que en el álbum Berling de Lurry, tenemos esa manera de contar historias que tenían Lurry en sus canciones, que es casi como que cada canción de Lurry es como una pequeña novela o una pequeña historia cerrada, como muy cotidiana, pero contada como muy de novela."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Tras los pasos de Lou Reed
facts.name: Berlin

facts.title: Theft of Bowie's Gear (1973)
facts.body: On July 2nd, 1973, after David Bowie's final Ziggy Stardust tour show at the Hammersmith Odeon Theatre in London, a young Steve Jones managed to get inside the building and steal microphones and amps. These stolen items would later be used by Jones to start his new band, the Sex Pistols, a couple of years later. "A young thief named Steve Jones somehow got inside and helped himself to whatever he could carry out, mostly some microphones and some amps."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 1
facts.name: Steve Jones

facts.title: Theft of Bowie's Gear (July 1973)
facts.body: As a young thief in July 1973, Steve Jones broke into the Hammersmith Odeon during a David Bowie and The Spiders from Mars' engagement and stole microphones and amplifiers. This gear is believed to have been used by Jones and the Sex Pistols in their early rehearsals and gigs starting in 1975, initiating their contribution to the punk rock era. "a young thief named Steve Jones broke into the theatre and made off with a bunch of microphones and amplifiers."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock
facts.name: Steve Jones

"It wasn't really even a given that he would be Danny Zuko in the Greece movie."

facts.body: This album resulted from David Bowie convincing Iggy Pop, the Ashton brothers, and James Williamson to come to England to make a record for Columbia Records. Despite Bowie's connection and influence, the album struggled commercially, peaking at 182 on the Top 200 charts. However, it deeply inspired many artists, including a 16-year-old Johnny Lydon and Mick Jones (The Clash) who were at Iggy's first UK show, and Kurt Cobain who later called it his favorite album. "But the people who bought this record were inspired."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: Raw Power

facts.body: This album was created with the patronage of David Bowie, who convinced his manager to invest cash into The Stooges project. The album was intentionally designed to be extremely intense, aiming to "actually hurt people as it came out of the speakers." It features the song "Search and Destroy." "The result was an injection of cash that was enough to make an album that was designed to be so intense that it would actually hurt people as it came out of the speakers."

facts.title: Appearance-focused Criticism (1973)
facts.body: A 1973 newspaper article from Tyler, Texas, titled "Women Country Singers far removed from their counterparts," focused heavily on Lynn Anderson's attractiveness on her album covers, illustrating how women in country music were often judged more for their looks than their musical talent. "The author goes on to say how attractive Connie Smith and Lynn Anderson are on their album covers."

facts.title: Appearance-focused Criticism (1973)
facts.body: A 1973 newspaper article from Tyler, Texas, titled "Women Country Singers far removed from their counterparts," focused heavily on Lynn Anderson's attractiveness on her album covers, illustrating how women in country music were often judged more for their looks than their musical talent. "The author goes on to say how attractive Connie Smith and Lynn Anderson are on their album covers."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 23 - Women of Country Music in the 70s
facts.name: Lynn Anderson

facts.title: Erotic and Socially Aware
facts.body: Released in 1973, this album featured liner notes written by Marvin Gaye himself, which included a quote from T.S. Eliot: "birth and copulation and death." While undoubtedly about sex, the album is also described as being as "socially and politically aware" as his earlier "What's Going On." Sociology professor Michael Eric Dyson praised it as a brave album for a black man to create such erotic content, directly countering the black exploitation films of the era by celebrating black sexuality, eroticism, and love. It reflects a part of the sexual revolution that viewed sexual freedom as beautiful, natural, and potentially a "gift from God." "Marvin Gaye released the Let's Get An On album in 1973."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 4 - Music of the 70s (Sexual) Revolution
facts.name: Let’s Get It On

facts.body: This debut album was released in August 1973. Despite the band being courted for a record deal and generating some buzz, the album failed to achieve widespread recognition outside of their immediate circle of fans. "The record deal came through in a self-titled debut record was released in August 1973, but outside of the band's immediate circle of fans, no one noticed."

facts.body: Released in 1973, this album was written entirely by Pete Townshend and tells the story of Jimmy Cooper, a young British mod. Jimmy, who quit his postal worker job to join the mod subculture, grapples with four distinct personalities, each symbolizing a member of The Who. Sean Murphy of *Pop Matters* (2011) lauded the album for covering universal rock themes like alienation, rebellion, redemption, sex, drugs, and rock and roll, alongside specific cultural references to mods, rockers, punks, and various personal struggles. An uncredited critic in the *Chicago Sun Times* (Fall 1973) compared its singular achievement to works like James Joyce's *Ulysses*, Beethoven's Symphony No. 9, and Goethe's *Faust*, describing it as "ever uncorrupted rock and roll, standing by itself in isolated splendor."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 42 - Rock Operas of the 70s
facts.name: Quadrophenia

facts.title: Retirement and Death (1950s-1973)
facts.body: Memphis Mini's health declined in the 1950s, forcing her to retire from music. A series of strokes eventually destroyed her ability to play the guitar, and she passed away in a nursing home in 1973. facts.title: Founder of CBGB (1973)
facts.body: Hilly Crystal, an ex-marine, opened the CBGB club in 1973 in the Bowery neighborhood of New York. Despite the area being an economic and social disaster zone at the time, the cheap rent allowed starving artists to live, rehearse, and create. Crystal established the club's musical policy, which fostered an environment where artists, "freaks, and weirdos" could do their own thing, leading to the birth of punk rock. "When an ex-marine named Hilly Crystal opened the place in 1973, it was in a part of town where nobody wanted to go."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Lasts
facts.name: Hilly Crystal

facts.title: CBGB Founding Vision (December 1973)
facts.body: Hilly Crystal, formerly the manager of The Village Vanguard, leased a former biker bar space in the Bowery, New York City, in December 1973. His original intent was for a venue featuring country, bluegrass, and blues music, which he named CBGB, adding OMFUG (Other Music For Uplifting Gourmandizers) to sound "uncouth or crude." "In December 1973, Hilly Crystal, the former manager of the village vanguard, he leased a space in the Bowery in New York City that was formerly a biker bar."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 57 - Punk and New Wave at New York's CBGB
facts.name: Hilly Crystal

facts.body: MCA Records, Newton-John's American label, strategically promoted this twangy, mid-tempo song to country radio first. It debuted on the Hot Country Singles chart in August 1973 at number 97 (her first appearance on that chart), slowly climbing to number 7 just before Christmas 1973. facts.body: Initially envisioned as a slow ballad by Gamble and Huff, this song was dynamically transformed by session drummer Earl Young. He significantly increased the tempo and introduced a "four-on-the-floor" beat with a prominent high-hat, an innovation that effectively created the foundational disco beat. "The session drummer Earl Young felt like it was dragging too much. So he sped things up with this four on the floor playing the bass drum on every beat and he hit that high hat symbol to drive the beaten holy shit."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.title: Brisbane Origin and Style (Late 1973/1974)
facts.body: Originating from Brisbane, Australia, The Saints began as Kid Galahad and the Eternals around late 1973 or 1974. Influenced by The Stooges and The Velvet Underground, they developed a distinctive fast-paced style, as they found they "couldn't play slow." By late 1975, they were performing their songs "really, really fast." "A band called The Saints released a rough, raw garage band like single that rocked in an entirely new way. They had obviously got their hands on some stooge's and velvet underground records."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 3
facts.name: The Saints

facts.title: Ambitious Film Project (1973)
facts.body: In 1973, at the age of 43, Dick Clark expressed a strong desire to produce a movie documenting the 20-year history of rock music. Although he was an entertainment mogul with various ventures by this time, the movie was never made. "In 1973, Dick Clark, who was 43 at the time, said he really wanted to do a movie about the time, 20 year history of rock."

facts.name: Dick Clark
